title: Ma- and Maka- verb forms
summary: Ma- and maka- verbs that show ability, and stressed má- and maká- verbs for accidental actions
goals: Understand what the prefixes ma- and maka- add to a verb root
Tell an intransitive ma- verb (active) from a transitive ma- verb (passive)
Form the past, present and future of ma- and maka- verbs
Use maka- to say someone is able to do something
Use stressed má- and maká- for unintentional or accidental actions

blocks.t: **Ma-** is a prefix attached to the **beginning of a verb root**. In general, a verb with ma- shows the **capability** to do something.
A ma- verb comes in **two types**, active and passive. Which one you get depends on whether the verb needs an object.

blocks.title: Two types of ma- verb

blocks.t: **Maka-** has the same meaning as ma-, except that maka- is **always active**. It takes a noun or a nominative pronoun (such as siyá and ikáw) as its subject.

blocks.title: Not every ma- verb has a maka- partner
items: A **ma-** verb can be formed from a verb showing **emotion or feeling** (to be angry, to be sad…).
A **maka-** verb can only be formed from a verb showing **action**.
So not all ma- verb forms have an equivalent maka- form.

blocks.title: Building the verbs
blocks.note: to sleep / to be able to sleep

blocks.t: An intransitive verb with ma- does **not need any other element besides the subject** to form a sentence. Its forms are made like this:

head: Form
Verb
How it is made
Meaning
rows: ma- becomes na- + duplicated first syllable + root
blocks.title: Ma- with an intransitive verb: túlog
Two simple swaps
items: For the **past and present**, ma- changes to **na-**.
For the **present and future**, the **first syllable of the root is repeated**: tú-tulog.

blocks.title: Examples of intransitive verbs using ma-

blocks.t: A transitive verb needs an object to complete its meaning. Its forms are made in the same way as an intransitive verb, **except that it has no imperative form**.

blocks.note: The accents are copied as the book prints this table. In its list of examples below, the book writes the infinitive as makita.

blocks.title: The subject takes the possessive form
blocks.t: Because a transitive ma- verb is passive, the doer is shown with a possessive pronoun such as **ko**, **mo** or **niyá**: *Nákíta **ko** si Mary* (I saw Mary).

blocks.title: Examples of transitive verbs using ma-

blocks.t: Generally, adding **maka-** to a verb expresses the **capability to do something** (to be able to). A maka- verb **does not have an imperative form**.

rows: maka- becomes naka- + duplicated first syllable + root
blocks.title: Maka- with túlog

blocks.t: The pattern is the same as ma-: **naka-** for the past and present, and the **first syllable of the root repeated** for the present and future.

blocks.title: Spot the subject
items: **Nagútom ako**: intransitive ma- verb, so the subject is the nominative pronoun **ako**.
**Nákíta ko**: transitive ma- verb (passive), so the doer is the possessive form **ko**.
**Hindi ako makaligò**: maka- is always active, so the subject is **ako**.

sections.title: Stressed má- and maká-: by accident

blocks.t: To express **unintentional or accidental actions**, attach a **stressed má-** or **maká-** to the beginning of a verb. These verbs show an act happening **beyond the control** of the doer or the receiver.

blocks.title: Stressed má- and maká-
items: The accent mark on **má-** and **maká-** is **kept in every tense**.
Not all stressed má- verbs have stressed maká- counterparts.

blocks.t: The forms are made like those of the unstressed ma-. But because the stress stays on **má-** in every tense, the **pronunciation is different**.

Which syllable repeats?
items: Ma- and maka- (ability): repeat the **first syllable of the root**: nakatú**tu**log.
Stressed maká- (accident): repeat **ka** from the prefix: naká**ka**tulog.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Ma- shows capability. Intransitive ma- verbs are active (subject: siyá, ikáw); transitive ma- verbs are passive (doer: niyá, mo).
Maka- means the same as ma- but is always active, and is only made from action verbs.
Past and present: ma- → na-, maka- → naka-. Present and future: repeat the first syllable of the root.
Transitive ma- verbs and maka- verbs have no imperative.
Stressed má- and maká- show accidental or unintentional actions, keep their accent in every tense, and have no imperative.
Stressed maká- repeats ka in the present and future: nakákatulog, makákatulog.

exercises.q: In general, what does a verb with ma- show?
exercises.explain: In general, a ma- verb indicates capability to do something.

exercises.q: A ma- verb made from an INTRANSITIVE verb is…
exercises.explain: It takes a noun or a nominative pronoun (siyá, ikáw) as its subject.

exercises.q: A ma- verb made from a TRANSITIVE verb is…
exercises.explain: It needs a subject in the possessive form, such as niyá or mo.
Maka- is always active and takes a nominative subject such as siyá or ikáw.

exercises.q: Why is there no maka- form of magálit (to be angry)?
options: Maka- is only formed from verbs showing action
exercises.answer: Maka- is only formed from verbs showing action
exercises.explain: Ma- can be formed from verbs of emotion or feeling; maka- cannot.

exercises.q: What is the past of matúlog?
exercises.explain: Ma- becomes na- + root.

exercises.q: What is the present of matúlog?
exercises.explain: Ma- becomes na-, and the first syllable of the root is repeated.

exercises.q: What is the future of matúlog?
exercises.explain: Ma- + duplicated first syllable + root.

exercises.q: Which verb form has NO imperative?
options: a transitive ma- verb such as mákita
an intransitive ma- verb such as matúlog
exercises.answer: a transitive ma- verb such as mákita
exercises.explain: Transitive ma- verbs and maka- verbs have no imperative.
Maka- becomes naka- + root in the past.

exercises.q: "Hindi ako ___ kung malamíg." (I cannot take a bath when it is cold.)
exercises.explain: Maka- shows the ability to do something.

exercises.q: In "Nákíta ko si Mary", why is the doer ko and not ako?
options: Transitive ma- verbs take a subject in the possessive form
Ako is only used in questions
exercises.answer: Transitive ma- verbs take a subject in the possessive form
exercises.explain: Like -in- verbs, a transitive ma- verb is passive.
The act is beyond the control of the doer or the receiver.

exercises.q: In stressed maká- verbs, what is repeated in the present and future?
options: ka, the second syllable of the prefix
the first syllable of the root
exercises.answer: ka, the second syllable of the prefix
exercises.explain: Nakákatulog, makákatulog.

exercises.q: What is the present of makátulog (to sleep unintentionally)?
exercises.explain: Maká- becomes naká- + duplicated ka + root.

exercises.q: "Nakápulot ang batà ng sampûng píso" means…
options: The child (by chance) picked up ten pesos.
The child will pick up ten pesos.
The child was able to buy ten pesos.
exercises.answer: The child (by chance) picked up ten pesos.
exercises.explain: Nakápulot: picked up, by accident.

recap: Ma- shows capability. With an intransitive verb it is active (subject: siyá, ikáw); with a transitive verb it is passive (doer: niyá, mo).
Maka- has the same meaning but is always active, and is only made from verbs showing action.
Tenses: ma- → na- (past, present) and maka- → naka-; the present and future repeat the first syllable of the root.
Transitive ma- verbs and maka- verbs have no imperative.
Stressed má- and maká- show accidental actions, keep their accent in every tense and have no imperative; maká- repeats ka in the present and future.
